name: Colin Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Brennick Moulding on Canal Road, the plant that makes plastic parts for cars, bumper covers mostly, some dashboard trim. I'm the lead on nights for line three, four big injection presses, which is where hot plastic gets shot into a steel mould and comes out as a part. My job is keeping them running, checking the first parts off each mould change, and catching the problems before they turn into a skip full of scrap. I like that I can hear when a press is wrong before the screen tells me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what keeps you there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Nights wear me out, and the heat off the barrels in summer. What keeps me there is the crew, honestly, and the fact that I'm the shop steward, so people come to me when something's not right with pay or safety. My partner Ines is a nurse, so between her shifts and mine we basically leave notes on the fridge. I'm twenty-seven and I've been there since I finished my two-year diploma.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right, so the boring version. That's fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say in the canteen: told you so. Every few years there's a new thing that's going to change everything, and we still end up with Dev and me changing moulds at three in the morning. I'd probably share some meme about it and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be a relief, but I'd know the robots on the presses are a separate story from the computer stuff. The pick-and-place arms that pull parts out of the moulds came in before I started and they'll keep coming whatever AI does. So hype or not, I'd still be watching the floor, not the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep putting money aside like now, about two hundred a month, and keep pushing at union meetings for a proper agreement on how new machines come in. Ines and I have talked about a bigger flat next year, and this version wouldn't change that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit smug, if I'm honest. Like when the weather warning comes to nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robot arms are a separate story. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The arm on press nine replaced a person who used to stand there pulling bumpers out and trimming flash, that's the extra plastic on the edges. Nobody was sacked, they moved Marta to inspection, but the job was gone. That happened without any clever AI, just a company deciding a machine was cheaper than her wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything about your work change at all in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the planning office gets some software to schedule the mould changes, and they'll pretend it's a revolution. We'll find out it schedules the big tool change for the same night two setters are on holiday. Then they'll ring me, like they do now.

S0.say: He'd tell the canteen he was right all along that AI was hype, and share a joke about it online. He'd point out that he and his mate are still changing moulds at three in the morning.
S0.think: He thinks it would be a relief but believes the robot arms on the presses are a separate threat that keeps coming regardless. He'd keep his eyes on the factory floor rather than the headlines.
S0.do: Keeps saving about two hundred a month and keeps going as normal at work. Keeps pushing at union meetings for an agreement on how new machines are introduced, and sticks with the plan for a bigger flat next year.
S0.feel: Calm and a little smug, like a storm warning that came to nothing.
S0.quote: That happened without any clever AI, just a company deciding a machine was cheaper than her wage.
S0.fieldNote: Colin separates software hype from the robot arms he already sees on the floor, and he worries more about the second. His union role colours everything; he frames change as decisions bosses make, not as technology. Even in the calmest picture he tells a story about a colleague losing her station.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds more like what's actually going to happen, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say: fine, but we negotiate it. No new machine goes on the line without a deal on what happens to the people who ran the old one. I'd be saying that in the branch meeting and to management's faces, politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm all right for a while because I'm the one who knows the presses best. But I'm not good with new tech. I've never even used one of those AI chat things, and if the job turns into watching screens and talking to software, the younger ones might be quicker than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd push the branch to get a technology agreement written before the first new system arrives, within six months. I'd bump savings from two hundred to three hundred a month and put the bigger flat off for a year. Courses, I'll be honest, I wouldn't sign up unless the company made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but there's a hum in the back of my head, like a bearing starting to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the technology agreement actually say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Simple things. If a job goes because of a machine, that person gets retrained on company time and keeps their grade for two years. And we get told six months before, not on the Monday the fitters turn up with the crates. We had that with the arms on press nine, nobody knew until the Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd push others to adapt but wouldn't take a course yourself. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I know. Ines says the same thing. I suppose I think my job is to protect people, and if I'm the best on the presses I'll be the last to go, so I've got time. That might be stupid. I'd probably only take the course if Dev did it with me.

S1.say: He'd say new machines are fine as long as the union negotiates the terms first. He'd say it in branch meetings and directly to management, insisting nobody loses out without a deal.
S1.think: He believes his skill on the presses buys him time, but he knows he's slow with new technology and has never used AI tools. He worries younger colleagues would outpace him if the job moved to screens.
S1.do: Pushes the union branch to get a written technology agreement within six months. Raises savings from two hundred to three hundred a month and puts the bigger flat off for a year.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a low background hum of worry he compares to a bearing starting to fail.
S1.quote: I've never even used one of those AI chat things, and if the job turns into watching screens and talking to software, the younger ones might be quicker than me.
S1.fieldNote: Colin admits a clear contradiction: he wants protections and retraining for others but won't take a course himself unless pushed. His confidence rests on being the best at a job that may itself change shape. The union is his main tool and his comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. Sorry, that just came out. That's basically tomorrow for a factory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need laws, and fast. Somebody's going to make a fortune out of this and it won't be anyone who works on Canal Road. I'd be posting about it, going to whatever demo there was, telling everyone to join the union now while it still counts for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'm finished in that job. The presses are already half robots. If you give the machine a brain that can do mould changes and spot a short shot, that's a part that didn't fill, then what am I for? I've got maybe three months of money and no other skill I could sell tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut spending straight away, no holiday, no new car, and try to get to four months saved before anything changed. Evenings would go on union work, pushing for a deal on redundancy pay and writing to the council and my member of parliament about some kind of income support. If the job went, I'd lean on Ines's wage while I worked out what came next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's moving. I'd be awake at noon when I'm supposed to be sleeping off a night shift, just staring at the ceiling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ines that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we might have to live on your money for a bit. And she'd say, of course, but I'd hate it. Then I'd probably say something about nurses being safe, and she'd laugh and say a robot can't do a night on a ward. I'm not sure that's true either in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta, who already lost her spot once. And Dev, he's got two kids and a car loan, he isn't like me with no kids. Me, I'd survive, I'd just be angry. Dev would be in real trouble inside a couple of months.

S2.say: He'd say this proves the need for urgent laws and that the profits won't go to workers. He'd post about it, join protests and urge everyone to join the union while it still has power.
S2.think: He thinks his job would be gone, since the presses are already half automated and a smart machine would replace his judgement. He has about three months of savings and no other skill he could sell quickly.
S2.do: Cuts spending at once, dropping holidays and a new car, and aims for four months of savings. Spends evenings on union work for redundancy terms and lobbies the council and his member of parliament for income support. Would lean on his partner's wage if the job went.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sleepless, feeling as if the floor is moving under him.
S2.quote: If you give the machine a brain that can do mould changes and spot a short shot, that's a part that didn't fill, then what am I for?
S2.fieldNote: The two-year version breaks Colin's belief that skill buys time. His anger points at owners and the lack of law, not at the technology. He worries more about a colleague with children than about himself, which fits his steward role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. So, I'd be thirty-two. Okay. That's a bit more room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but I'd say we've got time to do it properly this time. Get the rules in before the machines arrive, not after. I'd be on at the branch to start talking about a shorter week and shared gains, so if robots do the work, the money doesn't all go up the chain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think five years is just long enough for me to waste it. I know myself. I'd spend three years fighting and saying it'll never come to Brennick, and then it would. The difference is I'd have no excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, aim for six months of expenses by the end of year two. I'd stand for regional union rep if the role came up and push for a national campaign on workers sharing the gains. If Dev went on a maintenance course I'd probably go too, but I wouldn't go looking for one on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. It's the kind of nerves before a big mould change where you know what's coming and you've got your tools laid out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the most specific thing you'd do in the first year of those five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get a meeting with the plant manager, Mr Hollis, with the branch, and ask straight out what their plan is for 2031. Put it in writing. If he says there's no plan, that tells you everything. Then I'd take that to the members.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd waste the time. What would stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines, probably. She'd keep asking what the plan is. And maybe if someone I trust, like Dev, went first and said it wasn't bad. I'm not a first-in kind of person. I never was, not even with phones.

S3.say: He'd say there's time to get rules in place before the machines arrive. He'd push his branch towards a shorter working week and a fair share of the gains from automation.
S3.think: He fears he'd waste the five years telling himself it won't reach his plant, then be caught out. He says the difference from the fast version is that he'd have no excuse.
S3.do: Saves harder towards six months of expenses by the end of year two. Seeks a regional union role and campaigns for workers to share automation gains. Would join a maintenance course only if a trusted colleague went too.
S3.feel: Anxious but workable, like the nerves before a big mould change with his tools laid out.
S3.quote: I'd spend three years fighting and saying it'll never come to Brennick, and then it would.
S3.fieldNote: Colin is clear-eyed about his own tendency to dig in. The extra years mostly turn into more union work and more savings, not new skills. He relies on others, his partner and his colleague, to push him into change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole other life, nearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to win this. Enough to get a law that says if a robot takes your job you get a share of what it earns, or a proper retraining wage. I'd say that loud, in the pub, at work, wherever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think I'd still be on line three for most of it, because companies are slow and Brennick is slower. But at thirty-seven with nothing but presses on my CV, that's a bad place to be. The long version is comfy right up until the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep saving, keep going in the job, and spend the first year getting the branch signed up to a national campaign. Mostly I'd watch what other plants do before I changed anything myself. If I trained at all it would be late, and only if the company paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, sliding to anxious. Ten years makes it feel far off, and I know that's exactly the trap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing in year nine, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably still nights, but with fewer of us, maybe me and two others running what twelve used to. Looking at job ads in the evening and seeing nothing with my name on it. That's what scares me, not the robots, the evenings looking at ads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything about your plans with Ines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably go ahead with the flat, maybe even kids, because ten years feels like a normal life. But I'd want the deal written down before we had a baby. I wouldn't want to be the dad who got caught out.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is enough to win laws giving workers a share of what robots earn or a proper retraining wage. He'd say it loudly at work, in the pub and wherever else.
S4.think: He thinks he'd stay on the presses for most of the decade because his company is slow. But he sees that reaching thirty-seven with only press work on his CV would leave him exposed, calling the slow version comfy until the end.
S4.do: Keeps saving and keeps working as normal. Spends the first year getting his branch behind a national campaign, and mostly watches other plants before changing anything himself.
S4.feel: Uneasy edging into anxious, aware that the long timeline itself is a trap.
S4.quote: That's what scares me, not the robots, the evenings looking at ads.
S4.fieldNote: For Colin the longest timeline is the most dangerous because it lets him put things off, and he knows it. His fear is personal and concrete: evenings searching job ads with nothing that fits. He would carry on with family plans but wants protections in writing first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. Five and ten at least give the union a chance. What would help is a law that says when a company replaces you with a machine, you get paid while you retrain, a real wage, not a leaflet. And somebody making me do the course, honestly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who I'd blame. It's not the engineers. It's the people at the top who'll decide to buy the robots and keep every penny the robots save. A machine doesn't pick who gets the money. People do.

headlineQuote: A machine doesn't pick who gets the money. People do.
portrait: Colin Costa is twenty-seven, the night-shift lead on a line of injection presses at a car-parts plant and the union shop steward. He lives with his partner Ines, a nurse, and has around three months of savings. He has never used AI tools and admits he avoids anything new until someone he trusts goes first. He is calm when AI turns out to be hype, uneasy with steady change and alarmed by AGI in two years. Longer timelines mostly mean more union campaigning rather than new skills, and he knows the ten-year version is the one where he would be most tempted to wait.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two years leaves no time for the union to win anything.
whatWouldHelp: A law that guarantees a real wage while workers retrain when machines replace them, and, he admits, someone making him actually take the course.
